mergedJobs.answer:
First clarify what “twice as slow” measures, where the reported kernel duration comes from, and whether both runs use the same GPU, workload, clocks, driver/runtime, synchronization, warm-up, and repetition protocol. Matching kernel times don’t explain end-to-end time unless the timing boundaries and units are comparable; host submission, synchronization, transfers, compilation, or other work may be outside that kernel interval.

Run the same deterministic workload on both OSes and collect independent timestamps around each stage: process start, initialization, allocation, compilation, transfers, launch submission, explicit completion synchronization, and teardown. Repeat warm and cold runs, with and without transfers, and compare host wall-clock elapsed time against GPU event timing and device profiling traces—but treat each as a measurement to cross-check, not a ground truth. Add controlled delays and an empty-kernel case to test what each instrument includes, then reconcile stage totals with end-to-end wall time; the first stage whose measured duration diverges localizes the missing time, and disagreement between instruments flags a measurement-boundary or timer issue.

A directed graph has n vertices and m edges; one GPU thread per vertex performs BFS expansion. One frontier vertex owns half the edges. Design a work-efficient parallel expansion with duplicate suppression; prove work and span bounds under an explicit atomic-contention model.
mergedJobs.answer:
Use edge-parallel expansion within each frontier vertex, not one thread per vertex. Give each frontier vertex’s adjacency list to a CTA or a tile of lanes, with a grid-stride loop over edges; every lane tests its destination’s level via atomic compare-and-swap, and only the winner appends that vertex to the next frontier. For high-degree vertices, split the list into fixed-size edge tiles so the half-graph hub doesn’t serialize one thread; use a work queue or prefix-summed tile descriptors to schedule those tiles.

Assume bounded-degree-independent edge scans, O(1) atomic operations when uncontended, and a contention model where k simultaneous claims to one destination cost O(k) total work and O(log k) span via hardware serialization or a combining primitive. Each reachable outgoing edge is examined once, so expansion work is O(m_F), where m_F is the number of edges incident to the current frontier; duplicate suppression adds O(m_F) total contention work under that model, and successful discoveries append once. With P workers and balanced edge tiles, span is O(ceil(m_F/P) + log P + C_max), where C_max is the maximum contention cost for any destination; under the stated model C_max ≤ O(m_F), and under bounded fan-in O(log m_F). I’d need the specific atomic and scheduler model to claim a tighter worst-case span.

mergedJobs.question: An RDMA client crashes after posting a non-idempotent update but before observing completion. Can reconnecting and retrying guarantee exactly-once execution? Give an indistinguishability argument, then specify the minimal durable protocol state needed. Assume a ROCm wave64 executes LDS loads as two 32-lane transactions, with 32 four-byte banks and no broadcasts. Lane i loads word i·s. Derive conflict multiplicity for every positive integer s; prove your formula. A GPU benchmark is twice as slow on Windows as Linux, yet reported kernel durations match. What facts must you clarify first? Design a cross-platform timing experiment that localizes the missing time without assuming either timer is trustworthy.
mergedJobs.answer:
1. RDMA retry cannot guarantee exactly-once execution by itself.

Consider two histories: in A, the update executes and the client crashes before seeing completion; in B, the client crashes before the update executes. Without durable outcome information, these histories look identical to the recovering client. Retrying duplicates the update in A; not retrying loses it in B. A transport completion alone also does not establish application-level durable commitment.

The minimal durable protocol state is a stable operation ID retained by the client before posting, plus a server-side record binding that ID to the committed update and, if needed, its result. Recording the ID and applying the update must be atomic with respect to crashes, or recoverable through a durable log; otherwise a crash between them recreates the ambiguity. Retries reuse the same ID, and the server returns the recorded outcome instead of executing again. Deduplication records must survive as long as retries remain possible; safe reclamation needs an acknowledgment or fencing protocol that excludes old retries. A bare one-sided write does not provide this protocol automatically.

2. The conflict multiplicity is gcd(s, 32) per 32-lane transaction.

Let d = gcd(s, 32). Lane i accesses bank b(i) = i·s mod 32. Two lanes collide exactly when 32 divides s(i−j). Writing s = d·s′ and 32 = d·m, with gcd(s′, m) = 1, this is equivalent to m dividing i−j. Among 32 consecutive lanes, there are therefore m = 32/d distinct banks, each receiving exactly d accesses. Since s is positive, the word addresses are distinct, so no broadcast can reduce that multiplicity.

The second transaction has the identical bank pattern because (i+32)s mod 32 = is mod 32. Thus each transaction has d-way conflicts: odd strides are conflict-free, stride 2 has two-way conflicts, and multiples of 32 have 32-way conflicts. Do not combine the transactions into a 2d-way conflict; they are separate transactions under the stated assumption.

3. First clarify exactly what ‘twice as slow’ measures and what the reported kernel durations include.

Are we comparing end-to-end latency or steady-state throughput, and are synchronization, transfers, allocation, compilation, and warm-up included? Are the GPU, workload, outputs, launch count, batching, drivers, runtime versions, power settings, and competing workloads comparable? Also establish each timer’s source, resolution, boundaries, and synchronization semantics, including whether execution is asynchronous.

For the experiment, use identical validated workloads and repeated, randomized trials on both platforms. Measure long batches with a host monotonic clock, placing a device synchronization before the start and after the final operation. Separately instrument preparation, allocation, transfers, launch submission, completion waiting, and result processing. Collect device events and a CPU/GPU trace showing execution intervals, queue gaps, and scheduling; do not compare absolute timestamps across clock domains without establishing their mapping.

Treat every timing source as evidence rather than ground truth. Check host-clock elapsed time against an independent elapsed-time reference over long runs, and cross-check device events against trace intervals and batch scaling. Sweep iteration count, workload size, and batching, then remove transfers, reuse allocations, and compare asynchronous batches with per-launch synchronization. These controlled changes distinguish fixed setup costs, per-launch overhead, transfer time, and scheduling gaps. Agreement between independent measurements and predictable scaling—not matching kernel-duration reports alone—is what localizes the missing time.
